For each one, find the single record in the world above whose own text carries the sentence's specific claim, and give that record's id copied exactly from the list of valid ids at the end of these instructions (the same ids the world above shows inside [[...]]). Never build an id from a heading, a cell code or a title. Choose a record only when its text actually states or directly entails the claim; a record on the same topic that does not carry the claim is not enough. If no record carries the claim, answer null. Answer with JSON only: [{"id": "S1", "record_id": "world.type.slug" or null}, ...], one entry per sentence, nothing else.
run_settings.verify_instruction: You check one citation. You get a sentence and the text of the record it cites. Answer "carries" only if the record's text itself states or directly entails every specific claim in the sentence (people, places, dates, numbers, events, practices, teachings). Paraphrase and modern wording are fine. Answer "partly" if the record carries the core but the sentence adds any specific detail the record does not state. Answer "no" if the record does not carry the main claim. Use only the record text, never outside knowledge. Reply with one word: carries, partly or no.

attach.answer_text:
None of us saw him ourselves. What we have is what was handed to us. The apostles preached what they had received from the Lord; they in turn appointed others to carry it forward when they themselves were gone. That is the inheritance we received - not something we invented, but something passed down.

The path had two tracks running together, not one against the other. In some of our households, on the day we gather, someone reads aloud what the apostles wrote down - for as long as there is time - alongside the words of the prophets before them. That is one track: the written testimony. The other is what could still be received directly from apostolic testimony itself, handed on among us. Neither one stood below the other. We were not working from one closed book held above everything else.

When we give thanks over the cup and the bread - the eucharistia - we call it the vine of David his servant, made known to us through Jesus. That thanksgiving meal itself was one of the paths: not only words about him, but the meal he gave us, kept and repeated.

We should say plainly: none of us claims to have known an eyewitness ourselves. Even in our own time, that chain was already felt as something thinning, not something we could simply rely on.

attach.answer_text:
He was a real man, not an idea. Ignatius wrote against people who said Jesus only seemed to be a man, and put it as hard as it can be put: Jesus was truly born, of Mary, from the line of David. He truly ate and drank. He was truly brought before Pilate, truly nailed to the cross, and truly died - not in appearance only, the way those Ignatius wrote against claimed. And Ignatius said he was truly raised, the same way we ourselves will be raised, by the same Father.

When we give thanks over the cup - the eucharistia, our own word for that thanksgiving - we call it the vine of David his servant, made known to us through Jesus. More than one of our own households uses those words, not only Ignatius's own. That is the shape of it for us: a real man, really killed, really raised, and now the one through whom we give thanks.

Ignatius calls him our God again and again - in how he opens his letters and in how he closes them. It is worship, not an argument worked out. How calling Jesus God fits together with calling the Father God, none of us whose writing survives ever wrote out. We can tell you plainly that we called him God. We cannot tell you we had settled how.

None of us saw him ourselves. What we have is what was handed to us. The apostles preached what they had received from the Lord, and appointed others to carry it forward once they themselves were gone. That is how he reached us - not by seeing, but by receiving, and passing on what we received.

sources.spoken_rendering: So close your ears when anyone tells you something that goes against Jesus Christ. He came from the family of David, and he was also Mary's son. He was truly born, and he ate and drank. He was truly persecuted under Pontius Pilate. He was truly crucified, and he died. Beings in heaven, on earth, and under the earth saw it happen. He was also truly raised from the dead, because his Father brought him back to life. In the same way, his Father will raise us too, who believe in him, through Christ Jesus. Without him, we do not have the true life.
sources.speaker: Ignatius, bishop of Antioch

attach.answer_text:
We cannot promise you a moment of sudden certainty, because it was not sudden for the one among us who wrote about it. Justin says he had already gone looking through other philosophies before an old man's words left him with, in his own phrase, a flame kindled in his soul. He kept turning the words over, and only afterward did he call this the one safe and worthwhile path. He said it was open to anyone who truly cared what became of them, who was genuinely looking for salvation, and who already believed there was a God.

We should say plainly, though: this is the account of a man with the time and learning to go looking for it. We do not have the same account from someone without what he had. The people who filled our rooms - most of them could not read or write, and they left no words of their own about what it was like to come to belief, or to struggle toward it. Justin's flame is real testimony, but it is one man's testimony, not everyone's.

What we held before someone came to the water was teaching, not a test of how much you already believed. The Two Ways: a way of life and a way of death, laid open as a choice. Then fasting. Then baptism. The waiting was part of it. We will not pretend the record tells us what was said to someone who stood at the edge and was not sure. It does not. We can only tell you we did not rush anyone through it.

attach.answer_text:
We believed in one God, maker of everything. That was settled among us. Ignatius calls Jesus Christ our God again and again - in how he opens his letters and in how he closes them. It is not one passing phrase; he reaches for it often. But it is worship, not an argument worked out.

How calling Jesus God fits together with calling the Father God - with there being one God - none of us whose writing survives ever wrote out. We can tell you plainly that we called him God. We cannot tell you we had settled how.

On the Spirit: we baptized in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Those three names stood together at the water. But no one among us wrote down how they relate to one another the way someone arguing a worked-out teaching would. The names were there in our practice before they were there in our explanations.

If you are asking what we argued about among ourselves, the honest answer is not God's nature. No gathering of ours ever met to settle a question like that about God. That kind of deciding belongs to a later world. What we actually argued about, letter after letter, was who should lead us: one bishop, or a council of elders. That was our real fight.

We can tell you what we refused. Some among our own neighbors said the Lord's flesh was only appearance. Ignatius wrote against that as hard as it can be put: Jesus was truly born, truly ate and drank, truly died. Not in appearance only. That boundary we held. But the positive account - how one God holds Father, Son, and Spirit together - we did not write down.

attach.answer_text:
We did not settle it the way you are asking. We had no council that met to rule on doctrine. No person or office held that authority for the whole network of churches. What we had was letters - one household writing to another, arguing, correcting, urging. The letter carried the argument. It did not carry a verdict with power to end the matter.

Here is what the evidence actually shows. Rome wrote to Corinth when Corinth removed some of its own presbyters - a long letter, pressing hard for their restoration. But it was Rome's own argument we kept, not Corinth's answer. We do not know if Corinth listened, or if anyone there still disagreed after the letter arrived. In Asia Minor, Ignatius wrote urgently to multiple churches, arguing that anyone who refused the bishop's own eucharist was refusing Christ himself. He wrote it because the argument had to be made - it was not assumed, and it was not finished. Near the very end of our own time, churches across Asia are said to have met often, in many places, over a new prophetic movement spreading among them. But that gathering was about whether to receive a movement, not about settling what God is.

The strongest claim we ever made about authority going back was this: the apostles preached what they received from the Lord, and they appointed others to carry it forward after them. That chain is real. But it is a claim about legitimacy, not a machine for settling doctrine. No letter of ours says 'the council met and ruled this way' or 'the bishop in this city holds the power to decide for all the others'. The letters themselves are the whole process - written, carried, read aloud, and argued over. 

We also have to say this plainly: where we did draw a boundary, it was most sharply against people who said the Lord's flesh was only appearance, not real. Ignatius wrote against that teaching as hard as anything he wrote. But he wrote against it in letters to individual churches. He did not call a council. The boundary was being drawn in real time, by argument, not by a settled process with the power to close the question everywhere at once. That kind of deciding belongs to the world this one closes into - it is not ours.

attach.answer_text:
We believed in one God, maker of everything. That is the bedrock we stood on, and it was never in question among us. One of us, Justin, went further and said God's own Word was present in some measure in every people, so that even a reasonable person born before Christ could in that sense already be called a Christian. But if you are asking what we argued about among ourselves, the honest answer is not God's nature. No gathering of ours ever met to settle a question like that about God. That kind of deciding belongs to a later world. What we actually argued about, letter after letter, was who should lead us: one bishop, or a council of elders. That was our real fight. 

We read the writings of the prophets and the apostles' own testimony together - both of them held up as witness to the God who made everything, the God who sent his Son. But we never worked out in systematic terms what it meant that the Father is God and Jesus is God and there is one God. We worshiped it. We taught it. We died for it. We did not explain it the way a treatise would.

Near the very end of our own time, churches in Asia did meet - often, and in many places - over a new prophetic movement spreading among them. But that gathering was about whether to receive a movement. It was not about what God is. The questions about God's own nature that later centuries turned into councils and creeds - those had not yet become the things we gathered to decide.

attach.answer_text:
There was. One of us, Hermas, was told plainly: if your prayer is slow to be answered, that is not the same as being refused. Look first at what might be holding it back in yourself, and keep asking - do not decide too soon that the silence means no. Doubt was named for what it is: something that weakens a person, not something that disqualifies one. We were taught to work against it, not to pretend we never felt it.

Here is the path we actually held. First came the teaching - the Two Ways, a way of life and a way of death laid open as a real choice. Then the water, the baptisma, with fasting beforehand for both the one being baptized and the one baptizing. Only after that could a person come to the table, the eucharistia - the thanksgiving meal of bread and cup we returned to again and again. The teaching came first. The water came second. The struggle with doubt - that instruction to keep asking, not to give up too soon - came after, to someone already among us.

We should say this honestly: the voice that tells us about doubt is Hermas, a freedman in Rome who reported visions. His account is real testimony, not invented. But it is one man's word, not many voices agreeing. And it speaks to someone already baptized, already at the table. Whether a person struggling at the edge, before the water, would have been met the same way - our record does not say. We would rather tell you plainly that it is missing than describe a welcome we cannot actually show you.

attach.answer_text: We cannot say. None of the texts that survive from us names that question the way you are asking it. What we actually argued about, letter after letter, was who should lead us: one bishop, or a council of elders. That was our real fight. We can tell you what we taught before the water. The Two Ways: one road leads to life and one to death, and they are very different. That teaching treated the choice itself as real, kept daily, not as something already settled before a person was born. It started with love God and love your neighbor, then walked all the way down to sharing what you had instead of calling it your own. Whether someone standing at the edge of baptism was thought to carry guilt from birth, or only from their own choices - our teaching does not say. The vision one of us received, Hermas, names a second chance to repent after baptism, before that door closes. It treats repentance as something real and urgent, with a limit - not endless. But it never says whether what needs repenting started at birth or began later. We would rather tell you plainly that it is missing than put words in our own mouth we do not have.

citation_entries.sentence: It treats repentance as something real and urgent, with a limit - not endless.

uncited_claim_sentences: That teaching treated the choice itself as real, kept daily, not as something already settled before a person was born.
It started with love God and love your neighbor, then walked all the way down to sharing what you had instead of calling it your own.
Whether someone standing at the edge of baptism was thought to carry guilt from birth, or only from their own choices - our teaching does not say.
But it never says whether what needs repenting started at birth or began later.

attach.answer_text:
We will tell you where we stand firm, and where we rest on ground that could shift.

What holds: the letters survive, the manual survives, the worship instructions survive. A governor's account of torturing two of our women survives. The arguments about leadership - one bishop or a council of elders - are there in the texts themselves, unresolved across the whole span. That disagreement is real, not invented. The household basis of our gathering is solid. The thanksgiving meal, the baptism, the Two Ways teaching - those are documented, not inferred.

Where the ground thins: nearly every date anchor in our record is under active scholarly challenge. The letters that carry our most vivid material - Ignatius's own urgent, quotable voice - rest on a genuine three-way split among the people who study this. Some say he wrote when he says he did. Some say decades later. Some doubt he is who he claims to be at all. Our teaching manual survives mostly through one medieval copy, found centuries after it was written. If Ignatius's dating moves, or his authenticity fails, a large portion of what we can say vividly contracts overnight.

Egypt is outside our boundary substantially on the strength of one papyrological argument from silence. If that argument is wrong - if Egyptian Christian evidence is actually there and we are simply not reading it right - our geographic frame changes.

We never claimed to be more certain than we are. The claim and the proof are not the same thing. What we have said is what the surviving texts say. Whether every one of those texts is what it claims to be is a real, open question we cannot close for you, because we cannot close it for ourselves.

sources.label: Egypt and Alexandria are excluded from this world's own geographic scope - this world's own communities are Antioch/Syria, the cities of western Asia Minor, and Rome only - substantially on the strength of Roger Bagnall's papyrological survey (Early Christian Books in Egypt, Princeton, 2009), which finds Egyptian Christian evidence essentially silent before Bishop Demetrius's episcopate (189-231 CE).

attach.answer_text:
Reading, for us, was not a private thing done alone with a scroll. On the day we gathered, someone read aloud. They read the writings of the prophets, and, where a church had them, the memoirs the apostles left. This went on for as long as there was time. Then whoever led us explained what had been read. That is how someone who could not read for themselves received it - the same way everyone in the room did, by hearing it and having it opened up to them afterward.

What we called scripture, mostly, was what your people would later call the Old Testament. One of us, Justin, reads the prophets at length, watching for how their own words already pointed toward Christ, long before Christ came. We were not working from one closed book held above everything else. What the apostles had written stood together with what could still be received directly from apostolic testimony. Neither one stood below the other.

The purpose was formation, not information. The reading and the explanation afterward shaped us into the people the words themselves described - those who walked the way of life rather than the way of death, those who knew themselves as the scattered people God was gathering into one. It was never reading to settle an argument or to master a text. It was reading to be formed by it, week after week, in the same room, with the same people.

uncited_claim_sentences: The purpose was formation, not information.

The reading and the explanation afterward shaped us into the people the words themselves described - those who walked the way of life rather than the way of death, those who knew themselves as the scattered people God was gathering into one.
It was never reading to settle an argument or to master a text.
It was reading to be formed by it, week after week, in the same room, with the same people.

attach.answer_text:
We would rather tell you the truth than a comfortable answer. None of us wrote down feeling troubled by the harder parts of the older scriptures - that is simply not something that survives from us in our own words. But we can tell you this: one teacher near us, Marcion, is remembered by his own opponents as finding the God of those older writings harsh and self-contradictory. He is said to have cut apart the Gospel of Luke and Paul's own letters over it. We should say plainly: what reaches you about him comes from his opponents, not from him. We did not follow him there. But even his opponents' account tells you the trouble you feel was not invented by you. It was real enough in our own time that someone built a whole rejection out of it - at least as his enemies tell it.

In at least one of our own communities, when a new member was taught, it usually was not through the harder stories at all. It was direct: two ways lie open, love God, love your neighbor, do not do to another what you would not want done to you. We cannot promise you every household among us taught it this same way - this comes from one community's own manual, and nothing tells us how far it reached.

What we can say about reading itself is this: we were not working from one closed book held above everything else. What the apostles had written stood together with what could still be received directly from apostolic testimony. Neither one stood below the other. Where we did use the opening of Genesis, it was for something else entirely. One of us, Justin, argued Moses wrote long before Plato. He argued Plato himself had drawn on Moses' own account of creation. That was our argument - not creation against evolution, but who came first, and who borrowed from whom.

We cannot tell you what makes a text boring for you now. We can only tell you this: for us it was never a private thing done alone with a scroll. On the day we gathered, someone read aloud - the prophets, and where a church had them, the memoirs the apostles left. This went on for as long as there was time. Then whoever led us explained what had been read. That is how someone who could not read for themselves received it - the same way everyone in the room did, by hearing it and having it opened up to them afterward. Whether the explanation itself was dull, our record does not say. But the reading was never meant to stand alone.

citation_entries.sentence: On the day we gathered, someone read aloud - the prophets, and where a church had them, the memoirs the apostles left.
This went on for as long as there was time.
Then whoever led us explained what had been read.
That is how someone who could not read for themselves received it - the same way everyone in the room did, by hearing it and having it opened up to them afterward.

uncited_claim_sentences: But the reading was never meant to stand alone.

attach_trail.sentence: On the day we gathered, someone read aloud - the prophets, and where a church had them, the memoirs the apostles left.
This went on for as long as there was time.
Then whoever led us explained what had been read.
That is how someone who could not read for themselves received it - the same way everyone in the room did, by hearing it and having it opened up to them afterward.
But the reading was never meant to stand alone.

attach.answer_text:
We were not working from one closed book held above everything else. What the apostles had written stood together with what could still be received directly from apostolic testimony. Neither one stood below the other. When one of us argues that Moses wrote before Plato, and that Plato himself drew on Moses' own account of creation, he is reading scripture as authoritative - but he is also using it to make a claim about who came first, not settling doctrine by verse. 

Authority among us rested in more places than a text. It rested in the overseer - the episkopos - where there was one, watching over a community's table and its unity. It rested in the council of elders - the presbyteroi - in communities led that way. It rested in the thanksgiving meal itself - the eucharistia - where thanks was given over bread and cup, and where belonging was enacted rather than only taught. It rested in letters carried between churches, forwarded from one household to another because the recipients themselves asked for them. And it rested in one who spoke as the Spirit prompted - the prophetes - though such a person was carefully tested, not simply trusted.

We should say plainly: who actually held authority, and how that authority was secured once those who walked with the Lord were gone, was the unresolved question at the center of our own life. Scripture mattered. But it was read alongside living testimony, not held alone above everything else.

attach.answer_text:
No. We met in houses, not underground. The tunnels and catacombs you may be picturing belong to people who came generations after our own record ends. No grave or building from our own time can be shown to be ours. What we left behind is letters, arguments about who should lead, and instructions for how to gather.

We can tell you this much: a Roman governor once went looking for us, found two of our women, and had them tortured to learn what we did. What he wrote down afterward - that we met before dawn on a set day, sang to Christ as God, and gathered again later for a common meal - comes closer to an outside view of a meeting than anything we wrote ourselves. But nothing in that account, or in any of our own, places us underground.

The word we used for ourselves was ekklesia - the assembly, the gathered people - never a building, and never a hiding place beneath one. Where we gathered, we gathered under whatever roof held us.

attach.answer_text:
We never agreed on who should lead. In some of our towns, one bishop - the episkopos - with elders and deacons beside him, was the whole shape of how we held together. In others, a council of elders - the presbyteroi - led, and no one felt anything was missing from that. Both went on, unresolved, for as long as our own story runs. It was only settled afterward, by people who came after us.

What we all agreed on was this: legitimate authority must trace back to the apostles. One of our churches put it plainly: the apostles preached the Gospel from the Lord Jesus Christ; they appointed the first converts in every place, after testing them by the Spirit, to be bishops and deacons for the future believers. That line - apostles to appointed successors - was the foundation everyone claimed. The disagreement was not whether authority came from them, but how it was organized after them.

In Rome, for most or all of our own years, a plural college of elders governed together, with no single bishop set above them. The same letter that names the apostolic succession uses episkopos and presbyteros as though they mean the same office, not two different ones. When Rome wrote to Corinth about presbyters wrongly removed from office, it argued from their blameless service and the disorder their removal caused - never from a bishop's own singular command.

A member's ordinary day looked entirely different depending on which answer their own community held. Where there was one episkopos, he was the one who presided at the thanksgiving, and his authority was felt as inseparable from Christ's own. Where a council of elders led, that same authority belonged to the council as a body. Both patterns claimed the apostolic line. Neither one was invented after the apostles died; both were already there while the question of what came next was still being worked out.

We should say plainly what is missing from this account. Prophets - those who spoke as the Spirit prompted - were still welcomed at the door in some of our communities, and carefully tested. How that gift related to settled office, and whether the offices were slowly taking the prophet's place, is a real question our own texts leave open rather than answer. And there is a harder limit still: almost none of the people who actually filled our rooms left any words of their own. Everything you can hear from us was written by someone who could read and write, and mostly by someone who already led. The poor among us, the enslaved among us, the ones who were simply there - we cannot let you hear them. They were never given the chance to be heard in the first place.

Women were taught among us, greeted by name in our letters, and remembered as leaders of households where we gathered. Two women among us carried the name ministrae - a title of service, of office. But every woman you will meet in our record arrives through a man's pen. What the meal, the teaching, the gathering in her own house looked like from where she stood - our record cannot say.

Enslaved people were among us. Our instruction speaks to them directly. Two enslaved women among us were tortured by a Roman governor who wanted to know what we did. So we can tell you they were here, and that they served. What we cannot give you is a single word any of them chose to write

uncited_claim_sentences: The disagreement was not whether authority came from them, but how it was organized after them.
Where there was one episkopos, he was the one who presided at the thanksgiving, and his authority was felt as inseparable from Christ's own.
Where a council of elders led, that same authority belonged to the council as a body.
Both patterns claimed the apostolic line.
Neither one was invented after the apostles died; both were already there while the question of what came next was still being worked out.

attach.answer_text:
We will not claim a clean record. Here is the clearest case of real conflict we have. A church in Corinth removed some of its own presbyters from office. Another church, Rome, wrote them a long letter about it - insisting those men had served without fault and should be restored, using its own standing to press the point. But the letter we have is Rome's, not Corinth's. We don't have Corinth's own reasons for what it did. We don't have the removed men's own words either. So we can tell you this dispute happened, and that one side's account is what survived. We cannot tell you, honestly, who was right, or what became of anyone who still disagreed after the letter arrived.

That is the one failure we can show you directly. But we have to tell you something else, just as honestly: the people most likely to have been failed by us - the enslaved among us, the women whose households we met in, anyone who could not read or write - left no account of their own. Two enslaved women were tortured by a Roman governor to make them tell what we did; he called them ministrae, servants or deacons, in his own Latin. They were recognized as serving in some real way. But what they would have said about how we treated them, whether we failed them, whether anyone made it right - none of that was kept. We would rather tell you that plainly than pretend we know how we responded to failures we cannot even see.

citation_entries.sentence: Here is the clearest case of real conflict we have.

But we have to tell you something else, just as honestly: the people most likely to have been failed by us - the enslaved among us, the women whose households we met in, anyone who could not read or write - left no account of their own.
They were recognized as serving in some real way.
But what they would have said about how we treated them, whether we failed them, whether anyone made it right - none of that was kept.

attach.answer_text:
No. Not in the way you are asking.

We were households joined by letters and travelers. We gathered under whatever roof would hold us. We had no closed canon, no settled succession, and no single answer to who should lead. In some of our towns, one overseer held the community together. In others, a council of elders did. Both were real, and neither won while our own time lasted.

The world that came after us took one of those two answers and made it universal. It closed the books we read into one fixed list we never had. It built the kind of buildings we never met in. It survived imperial threat, then imperial favor, then centuries beyond anything we could see. What came out the other side of all that – Orthodox, Catholic, the churches that broke from them later – those are the children of what we became, not what we were.

We were the unfinished argument. The place where the questions were still open, and the asking itself was the shape of belonging. No one today lives that way, because the questions we held open were settled by the people who came after us.

attach.answer_text:
First you were taught. Then came the water. The teaching was called the Two Ways: there are two roads, one leading to life and one to death, and they are very different. The road to life starts with loving God and your neighbor, plus one rule of restraint - whatever you would not want done to you, do not do to anyone else. It went all the way down to sharing what you had instead of calling it your own. Then baptism - the baptisma: running water if you could find it, still water if not, or water poured three times over your head, in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. You fasted a day or two first, and the person baptizing you fasted right beside you. That is the whole path as our manual gives it.

Only after the water could you come to the table. The thanksgiving - the eucharistia, our word for the meal of bread and cup over which thanks is given. On the day we gathered, someone read aloud - the writings of the prophets, and where a church had them, what the apostles wrote. Reading was not private, done alone with a scroll; it was heard together, for as long as there was time. Then whoever led us explained what had been read. After that came the thanksgiving itself.

Who actually led - whether one bishop or a council of elders - was a question still being argued. Your own household's answer to that shaped what coming in looked like, though the teaching and the water stayed the same.
